name: Zane Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Zane. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Most evenings I deliver for my uncle's grill restaurant on Station Street, and when it's quiet I switch on one of the food apps and take other orders in my old saloon car. I start at four, finish around midnight, and Fridays and Saturdays are mad. I've only been at it just over a year, after the furniture warehouse closed, so I still get the side streets wrong. I'm engaged to Elif, and the wedding's next summer, so every extra order goes in the jar, as my mum calls it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out most, and what do you actually like about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The app wears me out, all the ratings and the little timers. My uncle's customers know me, but the app treats me like a number. What I like is the family side. My uncle feeds me at the end of the shift, my cousin works the grill, and I know if I'm short one month, they won't let me drown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, people got carried away with all these gadgets. At the restaurant we'd laugh about it. I don't post online much, but I'd say hard work still matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm relieved, because I don't use any of it and I don't want to. My worries are the wedding and saving for a deposit on a flat. AI was never going to pay for my wedding or a deposit on a flat either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my uncle's deliveries and the app on quiet nights. I'd keep saving for the wedding, about a third of what I earn. I wouldn't learn anything new, because nothing's asking me to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, mostly. A bit of pressure from the wedding, but that's a good kind of pressure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much of your money comes from your uncle versus the app?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About two thirds from my uncle, one third from the app. The app pays worse per order, but it fills the gaps. If the app vanished tomorrow, I'd be tighter, but we'd manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut if money got tight before the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own stuff first: the gym and the new phone. Not the wedding. Elif's family has plans, and I'm not going to be the one who lets them down.

I'd say **hard work** still matters more than any computer.
think: I'm **relieved**, because I don't use AI and don't want to.
My real worries are the **wedding** and a **flat deposit**.
do: Keep doing **uncle's deliveries** and the app on quiet nights.
Save about **a third** of earnings for the wedding.
feel: **Relieved**, with a good kind of **pressure** from the wedding.
S0.quote: AI was never going to pay for my wedding or a deposit on a flat either way.
fieldNote: His **uncle's restaurant** gives him steady work and a family safety net.

He's **resistant** to new tools and sees no reason to learn any.

steps.text: Keep driving deliveries for his uncle's grill restaurant
Put about a third of earnings in the wedding jar

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the big tech firms are getting too big, and it's office people who'll feel it first. I'd say people should learn a trade, something with their hands. At the restaurant I'd say thank God we cook real food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the apps get worse to work for, with more rules set by computers. My uncle's deliveries feel safer, because my uncle trusts me, not a program. If the app part shrinks, I lose about a third of my money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my uncle's deliveries and maybe ask him for more shifts. I'd cut the app nights if they got worse. I'd keep saving and wait and see before changing anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little uneasy. Mostly about the app side of things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your uncle's restaurant itself be affected?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe his ordering and his accounts, which his accountant does. My uncle doesn't trust computers either. He'd probably keep doing things his way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people should learn a trade. Would you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe one day. My dad always said get a trade. I'd think about the grill with my cousin, but I'm not in a hurry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the big tech companies have gone too far and it's ordinary families who'll pay. I'd say people need jobs, not handouts. At the mosque I'd hear the same from everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think by 2031 robot cars do takeaway too, even for my uncle, if it's cheaper. My thinking part is nothing, so it's all about when the robots come. Elif and I want kids by then, and I'd be thirty-two with no skills except driving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still have the wedding, but smaller, and put the rest towards the deposit. I'd ask my uncle to teach me the grill properly, starting now, so I'm in the kitchen not the car. I'd save every extra order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Afraid, honestly. Not for me so much, for the family we were going to have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a smaller wedding mean to the two families?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd be hard. Elif's mum has been planning for years. But I'd rather have a home than a big hall for one night. I'd talk to her dad first, man to man.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would robots come to the grill too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but I'd hope a family restaurant is the last place. People come to my uncle's for him, not just the food. That's what I'm betting on, anyway.

I'd say people need **jobs, not handouts**.
think: By **2031** robot cars deliver takeaway, even for my uncle.
I'd be **thirty-two**, maybe with kids, with only driving skills.
do: Have a **smaller wedding** and put the rest toward a deposit.

feel: **Afraid**, more for the **family** he hoped to have than for himself.

fieldNote: His fear is centred on the **family** he plans to start.
He'd move from the car to his uncle's **kitchen**, relying on family work.

steps.text: Hold a smaller wedding and move the savings to a deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so families and communities should get ready. I'd say firms should run apprenticeships, not just throw people out. That's how it used to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In private, five years means the wedding goes ahead as planned and maybe one child. Robots by 2034, I'd be thirty-five, with a young family. That's frightening, but there's time to learn the grill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving for the next few years and save. Around year two I'd start learning the grill on Sundays with my cousin. I'd want to be cooking full time before robots reach takeaway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but it's a slower worry. I'd still sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to hear from the government?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not money for nothing. I'd want them to pay firms to take on apprentices, like my dad's generation had. Give me a trade, not a cheque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Elif work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Elif works at the pharmacy, and she'd keep working, at least until the kids. I'd want her to have the choice. That's what a husband's supposed to provide.

I'd say firms should run **apprenticeships**, not throw people out.

Robots by **2034** catch me at thirty-five with a young family.
do: Keep driving and **saving** for the next few years.
Learn the **grill** on Sundays from around year two.
Move into **cooking** full time before robots reach takeaway.
S3.quote: Give me a trade, not a cheque.
fieldNote: He wants **apprenticeships** paid for by firms or government, not benefits.
His plan relies on **family**: learning the grill from his cousin.

steps.text: Keep doing deliveries for his uncle and the apps

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so no one should panic. I'd say families should stick together and plan. At the restaurant we'd probably joke about robot kebabs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels far away. I'd be thirty-nine in 2039, with kids at school. I'd want to be cooking or running something by then, not driving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go ahead with the wedding and the flat. I'd keep driving for a few years, then move to the grill. I'd keep saving like I do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled. A small worry, but family comes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn a trade, work hard, and stay close to family. That's what got me through. I'd say the same whatever the robots do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think robots will make kebabs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but my uncle's place will still be busy. People will still want an uncle who remembers your name and your order, and that's not something a machine sells.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Elif and I would be starting a family just as my job disappeared. What would help is apprenticeships, real ones, paid by the companies that profit from the robots. And for people to look after their own families, like mine looks after me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. At the mosque people help each other, and that matters more to me than any government scheme. I'd want those places to still be there, whatever happens.

headlineQuote: At the mosque people help each other, and that matters more to me than any government scheme.
portrait: Zane is a **27-year-old** takeaway driver for his uncle's grill restaurant, plus app work.
He's **engaged** to Elif, a pharmacy worker, and saving hard for the wedding.
He's **traditional**: trusts family and faith, wants trades, not handouts.
He's **resistant** to new tools and never uses AI.
He's **uneasy** in the slow pictures and alarmed when AGI arrives in 2028.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his job would vanish as they start a **family**.
whatWouldHelp: Real **apprenticeships** paid for by companies profiting from robots.
Strong **family and faith** communities that look after their own.
